aliases: Да Хун Пао с материнских кустов
cultivar: Da Hong Pao mother bushes (including Qi Dan)
processing: Hand-made in very small quantity as a Wuyi rock tea; the details of each year's making are not public.
harvest_season: No longer picked: harvesting stopped in 2006, and the last known picking was in 2005.
appearance_dry: Dark, twisted strips, as with other Wuyi rock teas; few people have seen it.
appearance_liquor: Presumably orange-amber like other Wuyi rock teas; little is recorded.
appearance_wet: Not reliably recorded; typical of the class, dark leaves with reddened edges.
taste_profile: No dependable tasting record is public. Anything offered as a description is either from a very few drinkers or marketing.

brewing.notes: The usual Wuyi approach, given here only for reference; you are very unlikely to brew the real thing. Try Qi Dan or Que She instead.

vintage_note: There is no new crop: picking stopped in 2006. Surviving tea is essentially off the market, and small amounts have fetched tens of thousands of yuan for 20 g at tea festivals. Assume anything sold under this name in a shop is not what it says.
description:
This is the tea from the original Da Hong Pao bushes on the cliff at Jiulongke in the Wuyi Mountains. It is the source of the name, and for ordinary drinkers it is no longer something you can buy.

There are six bushes, and genetic work groups them: numbers 1 and 5 match, 2 and 6 match and are known as Qi Dan, and 3 and 4 are each distinct. Local authorities stopped the picking in 2006 to protect them.

Tasting notes are not worth much here, because so few people have had verified tea. Rock tea character and roast are all that can reasonably be assumed.

If you see it for sale, be sceptical. To get close, drink Qi Dan or Que She, plants propagated from the mother bushes, and accept that they are descendants with different ground and age.
history:
A legend says an emperor recovered after drinking this tea and sent a red robe to drape over the bushes, giving the name; that is a story, not a record.

In 1962 Chen Dehua took cuttings from the mother bush, and the resulting cultivar was named Qi Dan. It was approved as a Fujian improved variety in 2012 and is treated as the pure line.

In 2006 the Wuyishan government halted picking and set the bushes aside for protection, which ended production.
